subject: Chemistry
title: How Matches Light
description: A quick win: understand How Matches Light.

hook.text: Strike a match and three chemical reactions happen in under a second—friction, ignition, and sustained burning.

buildup.text: The match head contains potassium chlorate (oxidizer), sulfur (fuel), and glass powder (for friction).

discovery.text: Striking creates heat through friction. The heat decomposes potassium chlorate, releasing oxygen that ignites the sulfur.

twist.text: Safety matches separate the chemistry: red phosphorus is on the box, not the match. They only light on the strip.

climax.text: Before safety matches, 'strike-anywhere' matches caused constant accidental fires—and were used in several murders.

punchline.text: Friction, oxidizer, fuel—in one swipe. Fire on demand.

quiz.question: How does striking a match start a fire?
options: Friction heats potassium chlorate, which releases oxygen to ignite the sulfur
The match head contains a tiny spark generator
Static electricity from friction creates a spark

details.summary: Safety matches work through a two-component system. The match head contains potassium chlorate as an oxidizer mixed with sulfur and glass powder, while the striking surface contains red phosphorus..
details.whyItMatters: Match chemistry illustrates oxidation reactions, activation energy, and intentional chemical design that separates fuel from ignition source for safety.
takeaways: Friction on the striking strip converts red phosphorus to reactive white phosphorus
Potassium chlorate in the head supplies oxygen to sustain the flame
Separating fuel and ignition source was the key safety innovation

faq.question: What is the difference between safety matches and strike-anywhere matches?
faq.answer: Safety matches separate the phosphorus from the oxidizer, requiring a special striking surface. Strike-anywhere matches contain phosphorus sesquisulfide in the head itself, so friction on any rough surface provides enough heat to ignite them..

faq.question: Why was the invention of safety matches so important historically?
faq.answer: Early matches used white phosphorus, which is extremely toxic. Workers in match factories developed phossy jaw, a devastating bone disease..
